headline: Land flipping in Florida: documentary stamps, the SAFE-Act loan-originator rule, and how Florida operators actually close
metaDescription: A working primer on land flipping in Florida — Florida’s documentary stamp tax on deeds and notes, F.S. §494 mortgage broker licensing, and the gotchas Florida operators run into.
intro: Florida is a high-volume state for vacant-land flipping, particularly in the rural interior counties (Putnam, Citrus, Levy, Highlands) and the cheap northwest panhandle. Florida’s legal framework around closings is friendlier than Texas’s in some ways — no annual statement requirement equivalent to Tex. Prop. Code §5.077 — but heavier in others. The documentary stamp tax (F.S. §201.02) hits every recorded deed at the closing table, and Florida’s licensing regime for anyone who originates a residential mortgage loan is enforced by the Office of Financial Regulation.
mechanics: A Florida land flip moves the same way: pull a list (the property appraiser’s office in each of 67 counties publishes a parcel roll), run mail, take inbound calls, run comps off the property appraiser’s recent sales tab, write offers. Florida closings happen either at a title company or a real-estate attorney’s office — both are common — and use a Florida-form general warranty deed or a special warranty deed. When seller financing comes in, the operator can use either a note + mortgage (recorded as a mortgage with the clerk of court) or an agreement-for-deed (Florida’s analog to Texas’s executory contract). Florida case law has historically been less protective of agreement-for-deed buyers than Texas statute, but Mid-State Investment v. O’Steen and subsequent cases pushed Florida courts toward treating long-term agreements-for-deed as equitable mortgages — meaning a defaulted buyer with substantial equity in is owed a foreclosure rather than self-help cancellation.

statutes.headline: F.S. §201.02 — documentary stamp tax on deeds
statutes.body: Florida levies a documentary stamp tax of $0.70 per $100 of consideration on every deed recorded statewide (Miami-Dade is $0.60 per $100 plus a $0.45 per $100 surtax for non-single-family). The tax is collected by the clerk of court at recording. On a $20,000 raw-land flip, that’s $140 paid at the closing table. A flipper running 30 closings a year is writing roughly $4,200 in doc stamps. The same statute applies to assignments of contract — wholesalers who structure as double-closes pay doc stamps twice.

statutes.headline: F.S. §201.08 — documentary stamp tax on promissory notes
statutes.body: Florida also levies a $0.35-per-$100 doc stamp on the face amount of every promissory note executed or delivered in Florida. A $25,000 seller-financed note carries an $87.50 stamp tax at execution. Sellers who fail to affix the stamp render the note unenforceable in Florida courts until the tax is paid plus penalty. Operators running a note book in Florida need to budget this into the per-deal close cost.

statutes.headline: F.S. Chapter 494 — Loan Originator and Mortgage Broker licensing
statutes.body: Florida’s SAFE-Act implementation (F.S. §494.0011-§494.00125) requires a license to originate residential mortgage loans on Florida property. The seller-financing exception is narrow: F.S. §494.00115(2)(a)(3) exempts a natural-person seller who finances the sale of their own residence in any 12-month period — but commercial sellers (including most LLCs) and serial-finance operators do not qualify. Land flippers selling raw vacant land are generally outside the residential-mortgage definition; flippers seller-financing a home with the lot are not. The OFR’s enforcement actions against unlicensed serial seller-financers have included six-figure fines.

statutes.headline: Florida case law on agreements-for-deed
statutes.body: Florida courts have repeatedly held that long-term installment land contracts can be treated as equitable mortgages, triggering full judicial foreclosure rather than the simple eviction the seller wrote into the contract (see Hoffman v. Semet, H&L Land Co. v. Warner, Hidden Harbour v. Allied Riggers). Operators relying on agreement-for-deed for the eviction speed should run that assumption past Florida counsel — a default on year 7 of a 10-year agreement is more likely to require a Chapter 702 foreclosure than a Chapter 83 eviction.

statutes.headline: F.S. §197.502 — tax-deed redemption
statutes.body: Florida tax deeds are issued through a clerk-of-court auction after a tax certificate has been outstanding for at least two years. The redemption right ends the moment the tax deed is issued — there is no post-sale statutory redemption period the way Texas has. Buyers at a Florida tax deed auction take immediate title, subject to any pre-existing governmental liens and certain pre-existing mortgages. Operators flipping tax-deed acquisitions in Florida have a cleaner timeline than operators flipping Texas tax sales.

gotchas.headline: Homestead exemption fights add risk in Florida
gotchas.body: Florida’s constitutional homestead protection (Fla. Const. art. X §4) is broader than most states’. If the buyer claims homestead on a parcel sold under agreement-for-deed, the seller’s remedy gets harder. Verify the buyer’s homestead status at the property appraiser before structuring the deal.

gotchas.headline: The clerk-of-court is the recording office, not the property appraiser
gotchas.body: Florida flippers regularly confuse the two. The property appraiser publishes parcel rolls + assessed values. The clerk of court records deeds, mortgages, and lien filings. They are separate elected offices in each of 67 counties, with separate websites, search interfaces, and fee schedules.

gotchas.headline: Florida has no state income tax, but counties levy non-ad-valorem assessments
gotchas.body: A parcel with a special-district assessment (CDD, fire, mosquito control) carries an annual lien that runs with the land. The seller financing such a parcel and escrowing taxes is also escrowing the non-ad-valorem assessment. Missing it once at closing and the buyer is paying it as 'a surprise' the following year.

gotchas.headline: Quiet-title actions are common for tax-deed parcels
gotchas.body: A Florida tax-deed acquisition is technically merchantable but most title insurers will not insure it for 3-4 years post-deed without a quiet-title action under F.S. §65.011. Operators flipping tax-deed acquisitions should budget for a quiet-title suit (~$1,500-$3,500 in attorney fees + court costs) if they want to deliver a title-insurable parcel to the next buyer quickly.

valueProp: AcreOS ships with the Florida-specific closing-cost worksheet built into the deal record — doc stamps on deeds, doc stamps on notes, recording fees, and non-ad-valorem assessment lookup are all pulled from F.S. §201 and the clerk-of-court fee schedule per county. The mortgage-vs-agreement-for-deed decision surfaces in the deal worksheet with the equitable-mortgage risk flagged. Pax watches the Florida county tax-deed calendars and surfaces auction dates 30 days out per county. The Florida county registry is pre-loaded across all 67 counties.

faq.q: Do I need a license to flip land in Florida?
faq.a: Not to sell your own parcels. F.S. Chapter 475 regulates real-estate brokers acting on behalf of others; a principal selling their own property is exempt. The licensing question changes if you’re originating residential mortgage loans on the financed sale of a home (see F.S. Chapter 494).

faq.q: Who pays Florida doc stamps at closing?
faq.a: By Florida custom the seller pays the deed doc stamp; the buyer pays the note doc stamp and intangible tax (F.S. §199 — repealed for non-recurring intangibles in 2007 but still applicable in narrow cases). The parties can contract otherwise but the clerk collects from whoever shows up at recording.

faq.q: Are wraparound mortgages legal in Florida?
faq.a: Yes, but the underlying note’s due-on-sale clause is enforceable in Florida (F.S. §697.061 allows acceleration). Wraps on Florida land where the underlying lender is paying attention are real-world risky.

faq.q: How fast can I resell a Florida tax-deed property?
faq.a: Immediately — there’s no post-sale redemption. The blocker is title insurability. Most insurers want a four-year cure period or a quiet-title action under F.S. §65.011 before they’ll insure.

faq.q: What does a Florida property-appraiser parcel record give me?
faq.a: Owner name + mailing address, legal description, assessed value, taxable value, year built (if improved), zoning, recent sale history (with deed-recording details), and the homestead-exemption flag. It’s the foundation of most Florida land flippers’ list-building.

faq.q: Are there county-by-county recording fee differences in Florida?
faq.a: Yes — F.S. §28.24 sets the floor at $10 for the first page, $8.50 each additional page, but counties layer service charges. Miami-Dade and Broward routinely run higher. AcreOS pre-loads the per-county fee schedule into the closing worksheet.

faq.q: Do I owe Florida sales tax on a vacant-land flip?
faq.a: Sales of real property are not subject to Florida sales tax. The transfer tax is the documentary stamp under F.S. §201.
